analysis.one_liner: Bans online platforms from microtargeting political ads using personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2021 with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped large online platforms from using personal data to aim political ads at specific individuals, devices, or groups. Campaigns could still target ads by place — a state, a city, a congressional district — or to people who consented or were already searching for related content, but they could not single people out based on browsing history, profiles, or purchased data lists. It also gave individuals the right to sue platforms that broke the rule and extended campaign finance disclosure rules to paid online political ads.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would benefit from a political information environment that looks more like broadcast TV: everyone in a state or district sees roughly the same political messages, rather than each person receiving ads tuned to their individual profile. It would also give voters a practical tool — the right to sue, with damages and attorney's fees, and no forced arbitration — if platforms kept microtargeting anyway. Smaller platforms with data on fewer than 50 million people are exempt [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters exposed to targeted political ads

how_it_helps.text: It generally prohibits covered online platforms and political ad sponsors from targeting political ads to individuals, devices, or groups based on personal information, allowing targeting only by recognized place (such as a state or congressional district), with the person's express consent, contextually (based on what the person is viewing or searching), or on a random basis.

It gives individuals the right to sue platforms that violate the ban, with damages of $100–$1,000 per violation for negligent conduct and $500–$5,000 for willful violations, plus attorney's fees — and it bars platforms from forcing users into pre-dispute arbitration or blocking class actions over these claims.

It closes a disclosure loophole by expanding the definition of 'electioneering communication' to include paid internet and digital ads, so online political ads are subject to the same campaign finance disclosure rules as broadcast ads.

analysis.who_pays: Large online platforms and ad-tech companies (those handling data on 50 million or more people) would lose the ability to sell individually targeted political advertising, one of their most lucrative products, and would face private lawsuits for violations. Political data brokers and targeting vendors would lose the market for selling voter lists and device identifiers. Campaigns would lose the ability to cheaply and precisely reach narrow voter segments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media and ad-tech platforms

drawbacks.text: Banning individual-level targeting applies to all political advertising, including ads from small campaigns and grassroots groups that used cheap, precise digital targeting to reach voters; those advertisers would lose a low-cost tool along with the large platforms.

The bill creates a private right of action allowing any individual to sue platforms for $100–$5,000 per violation, which could generate substantial litigation against online platforms and, in the view of critics of such provisions, be used to pressure speech-adjacent businesses.

Expanding the definition of electioneering communication to include paid internet and digital communications subjects more online political speech to federal campaign finance rules, which some would object to as a burden on political expression.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — fewer manipulative, individually targeted political ads — is real but comes with trade-offs an honest supporter would acknowledge. Narrowing political ads to place-based targeting pushes campaigns toward broadcast-style messaging, which can raise costs for small campaigns and grassroots groups that used cheap microtargeting to reach niche audiences, not just for deep-pocketed advertisers. The private right of action with damages and fee-shifting is a strong enforcement tool, but it could also invite litigation against platforms over borderline cases. The bill never received any committee or floor consideration, so none of these questions were ever aired or weighed.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Administration Committee from August 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023, and the committee never took it up.

narrative.text: Eshoo introduced H.R. 4955 on August 6, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration.
No member of the House joined as a cosponsor; the bill had zero cosponsors for its entire life.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online platforms and the political data-targeting industry keep selling individually targeted political ads untouched; no restrictions ever took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large online ad platforms and data brokers

for.name: Rep. Anna G. Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 6, 2021; it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the 16 months it had jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat and drew no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split ever took shape; it simply never moved.

industries.industry: Digital advertising platforms and ad networks (social networks, search engines, ad-tech)
industries.note: The bill prohibits them from selling individually targeted political advertising based on personal data, a high-margin product, and exposes them to private lawsuits with per-violation damages. Platforms with data on fewer than 50 million people are exempt, so the burden falls on the largest companies.

industries.industry: Political data brokers and ad-targeting vendors
industries.note: The bill bars platforms from handing third parties lists of individuals, contact information, or device identifiers for political ad targeting, cutting off the market for political microtargeting data.

Campaigns would lose precise, inexpensive voter targeting for political ads, but everyone would compete on equal, broadcast-style footing and online ads would face the same disclosure rules as TV, which campaigns on both sides already navigate.
